  "title": "Calibrated Surprise Gating: Repurposing World Models for Selective Verification in Multi-Step Agent Loops",
  "core_problem": "LLM agents face a self-verification dilemma: universal self-verification is mostly confirmatory and wasteful (arXiv:2602.03485), while absent verification misses critical errors. Recent work has produced high-quality world models for agents—WebWorld (arXiv:2602.14721) trains open-weight 8B/14B/32B next-state predictors on 1M+ web trajectories, and RWML (arXiv:2602.05842) learns action-conditioned world models via sim-to-real gap rewards. However, these world models are used exclusively for training-time purposes: data synthesis, lookahead action selection, or reward shaping. No work has studied how to repurpose existing world models as online verification gates during agent execution. DyMo (arXiv:2506.02918) integrates prediction into the backbone for single-turn self-verification sampling, but couples prediction to a specific backbone and does not extend to multi-step trajectories. Sherlock (arXiv:2511.00330) addresses selective verification in DAG-structured workflows via offline counterfactual analysis, but requires pre-defined workflow graphs. The prediction-observation mismatch principle for anomaly detection is established in robotics MBRL (arXiv:2503.02552), and Trajectory Guard (arXiv:2601.00516) provides lightweight anomaly detection for agent trajectories via Siamese autoencoders. The open question is: can existing world models be repurposed—with principled calibrated confidence gating—as model-agnostic, online verification gates for multi-step tool-use agent loops, and does this outperform both universal verification and no verification?",
  "opportunity": "High-quality pre-trained world models now exist as open-weight artifacts (WebWorld-8B achieves simulation quality comparable to Gemini-3-Pro), but their use has been limited to training data synthesis and inference-time action selection. We observe that these models contain a latent signal that has been overlooked: calibrated prediction surprise. When a world model's predicted next state diverges from the actual environment observation, this surprise signal indicates the agent has entered an unexpected situation—precisely when verification is most valuable. The prediction-observation mismatch principle is proven effective for anomaly detection in robotics RL (arXiv:2503.02552), but applying it to LLM agents requires solving two challenges that do not arise in continuous-state RL: (1) structured textual states (A11y trees, HTML) require semantic rather than Euclidean distance for mismatch measurement, and (2) world model confidence in text generation is poorly calibrated out-of-the-box (trained for simulation fidelity, not uncertainty quantification), necessitating post-hoc calibration for principled gating thresholds. Crucially, this approach uses prediction for anomaly detection (detecting unexpected outcomes)—a fundamentally weaker assumption than using prediction for planning or foresight, directly sidestepping the failure mode identified in arXiv:2601.03905 where agents fail to leverage world models for action selection. Unlike WAC (arXiv:2602.15384) which uses heuristic confidence thresholds on a prompted (untrained) world model, we propose calibrated gating on a trained world model with cost-sensitive threshold optimization.",
  "landscape": "Huang et al. (2023, arXiv:2310.01798) showed LLMs cannot reliably self-correct reasoning. The self-verification dilemma paper (arXiv:2602.03485, Feb 2026) empirically demonstrated that recheck behaviors are predominantly confirmatory, motivating selective approaches. **World models for agents**: WebWorld (arXiv:2602.14721, Qwen team, Feb 2026) trains open-weight 8B/14B/32B next-state predictors on 1M+ real web trajectories, achieving Gemini-3-Pro-level simulation quality and enabling +9.2% WebArena gains via synthetic training data—but is designed for training data synthesis and lookahead search, not verification gating. DyMo (arXiv:2506.02918, Guo et al., June 2025) trains dynamics modeling into a backbone LLM via SFT+RL for Self-Verification Sampling on single-turn function calls (BFCL-V2)—but tightly couples prediction to the backbone (Cohere R7B) and does not extend to multi-step trajectories. RWML (arXiv:2602.05842, Microsoft, Feb 2026) learns action-conditioned world models via sim-to-real gap rewards in embedding space, achieving +6.9/+5.7 on ALFWorld/τ²-Bench—but uses prediction-reality alignment as a training signal for improving the agent, not as an inference-time verification gate. WAC (arXiv:2602.15384, Feb 2026) augments web agents with a prompted (untrained) world model using simple confidence thresholds for action correction—but lacks calibrated confidence and uses heuristic thresholds. SafePred (arXiv:2602.01725, Feb 2026) uses world models as predictive safety guardrails for computer-using agents but focuses on risk prediction rather than execution verification. ForeAgent (arXiv:2601.05930, Jan 2026) implements predict-then-verify with confidence gating for ML pipeline agents specifically. **Anomaly detection in agents**: Trajectory Guard (arXiv:2601.00516, Jan 2026) achieves 0.88–0.94 F1 at 32ms latency for real-time anomaly detection in agent trajectories via a Siamese recurrent autoencoder—architecturally different (trajectory embeddings vs. world-model predictions) and does not leverage environment dynamics knowledge. In robotics RL, arXiv:2503.02552 (Mar 2025) directly proposes prediction-observation mismatch from world models for anomaly detection with error thresholds—the core mechanism we adapt to LLM agents, but applied in continuous-state robotics rather than structured-text agent environments, and without calibrated confidence. **Selective verification**: Sherlock (arXiv:2511.00330, Microsoft, Nov 2025) achieves selective verification in DAG-structured agentic workflows via offline counterfactual fault injection—but requires pre-defined workflow graphs, not applicable to dynamic sequential agent loops. HTC (arXiv:2601.15778, Salesforce, Jan 2026) extracts 48-dimensional trajectory features for post-hoc confidence estimation—but operates after trajectory completion, not online during execution. CSO (arXiv:2602.03412, Feb 2026) identifies verified critical steps in hindsight via a PRM, operating post-hoc. AgentPRM (arXiv:2511.08325, ACM WWW 2026) provides step-level process reward models for beam search guidance. **Meta-landscape**: The Agentic World Modeling survey (arXiv:2604.22748, Apr 2026) catalogs 400+ works across an L1 Predictor → L2 Simulator → L3 Evolver taxonomy. Our contribution is NOT building a new L1 Predictor (WebWorld already excels at this) but rather demonstrating a novel application of L1 Predictors: using their calibrated surprise signal as an online verification gate—a use case not identified in the survey's taxonomy. arXiv:2601.03905 (UIUC, Jan 2026) shows agents fail to leverage world models for planning (<1% simulation invocation, ~15% misuse)—but these failures are about using prediction for action selection; our approach uses prediction only for anomaly detection, a fundamentally weaker assumption. **The gap**: No work combines (1) a pre-trained world model repurposed for verification rather than training/search, (2) calibrated confidence via post-hoc temperature scaling for principled gating thresholds, and (3) online prediction-reality mismatch detection with cost-sensitive threshold optimization for multi-step agent trajectories.",
  "approach": "We propose Calibrated Surprise Gating (CSG), a model-agnostic verification gating mechanism that repurposes existing world models as online anomaly detectors for multi-step agent loops. The key insight is that pre-trained world models like WebWorld contain a latent surprise signal—calibrated prediction-reality divergence—that can serve as a principled trigger for selective verification without modifying the backbone agent.\n\n**Predictor**: Deploy WebWorld-8B (frozen, open-weight) as the observation predictor. Given state history and the action just executed, WebWorld-8B predicts the expected next page state in A11y tree format. No predictor training is required—we leverage WebWorld's 1M+ trajectory pre-training directly. This makes the approach immediately deployable with any backbone agent.\n\n**Calibration pipeline**: WebWorld-8B was trained for simulation fidelity, not uncertainty quantification—its raw softmax confidences are miscalibrated for gating decisions. We apply temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017; Thermometer, arXiv:2403.08819) on a held-out calibration set of ~200 WebArena trajectories collected by running the backbone agent. The temperature parameter T is optimized to minimize Expected Calibration Error (ECE) on the held-out set. We also evaluate Platt scaling and isotonic regression as calibration alternatives in ablations.\n\n**Dual gating criteria**: At each agent step: (1) the backbone executes an action and receives the actual environment observation; (2) WebWorld-8B generates the predicted observation; (3) we compute two signals: (a) calibrated prediction entropy from the temperature-scaled softmax distribution (capturing predictor uncertainty), and (b) prediction-reality semantic divergence using sentence-transformer cosine distance between predicted and actual A11y tree representations (capturing factual mismatch). Verification triggers when either signal exceeds its respective threshold.\n\n**Cost-sensitive threshold optimization**: Rather than choosing thresholds heuristically (as in WAC), we formulate threshold selection as cost-sensitive binary classification. On the calibration set, we label each step as 'error-relevant' (step where the agent's action leads to eventual task failure and verification could have caught it) or 'nominal,' then optimize thresholds τ_entropy and τ_divergence to minimize a weighted loss: λ_FP × false_positive_rate + λ_FN × false_negative_rate, where λ_FN > λ_FP reflects that missed errors are costlier than unnecessary verification. This yields principled, task-aware thresholds rather than ad-hoc cutoffs.\n\n**Structured verification subroutine**: When gating triggers, instead of free-form self-rechecking (which is confirmatory per arXiv:2602.03485), we present the backbone with a structured prediction-reality diff highlighting specific discrepancies between WebWorld's prediction and the actual observation. The backbone performs targeted re-examination of the flagged discrepancies and may revise its next action. This replaces open-ended 'did I make a mistake?' prompts with focused 'the world model expected X but observed Y—is this a problem?' queries.\n\n**Overhead analysis**: WebWorld-8B inference requires ~50–100ms per step on A100 (short A11y tree context). Sentence-transformer embedding + cosine similarity adds ~10ms. A backbone agent step (Qwen3.5-27B) with browser interaction takes 3–10 seconds. CSG adds ~1–3% per-step latency overhead. Full verification (a second backbone call) costs 3–10 seconds. If CSG triggers verification at ~20–30% of steps (vs. 100% in always-verify), the net compute saving is ~60–75% of verification cost minus the small predictor overhead.\n\n**Evaluation**: WebArena Verified-Hard (258-task subset) using Qwen3.5-27B as the primary backbone agent. Baselines: (1) never-verify (no self-check), (2) always-verify (free-form self-recheck at every step), (3) random-gated (verify at random ~25% of steps), (4) HTC-online (adapt HTC's 48-dimensional trajectory features for step-wise online confidence estimation), (5) entropy-only (WebWorld prediction entropy without reality comparison—ablation isolating the value of the mismatch signal). Metrics: task success rate, verification trigger rate, gating precision/recall against oracle step labels, and end-to-end wall-clock time. Optional stretch experiment: run a 50-task subset with Llama-4-Scout as backbone to validate model-agnosticity.\n\n**Ablations**: (1) calibration methods: temperature scaling vs. Platt scaling vs. isotonic regression vs. uncalibrated; (2) mismatch metrics: sentence-transformer cosine vs. BERTScore vs. token-level F1 on A11y tree; (3) predictor size: WebWorld-8B vs. WebWorld-14B (does larger predictor improve gating?); (4) threshold sensitivity analysis across λ_FN/λ_FP ratios; (5) entropy-only vs. divergence-only vs. combined gating.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 3)
Issues: ["CRITICAL: WebWorld-8B has a documented sycophancy bias—the WebWorld paper itself notes it 'generates overly optimistic outcomes that cater to the agent's action.' This directly undermines CSG's core mechanism: a sycophantic world model will predict that the agent's action succeeded even when it didn't, producing LOW surprise scores at exactly the moments verification is most needed. The proposal uses WebWorld-8B as a frozen predictor without addressing this known failure mode. Calibration via temperature scaling adjusts confidence magnitudes but cannot fix systematic directional bias (sycophancy is a bias in predicted content, not in confidence calibration). This must be addressed—either by (a) fine-tuning the predictor with anti-sycophancy objectives, (b) using contrastive decoding that suppresses sycophantic predictions, (c) empirically measuring sycophancy rates on the calibration set and reporting them, or (d) switching to WebWorld-14B/32B if they exhibit less sycophancy.", "Novelty concern: WAC (arXiv:2602.15384) already deploys a world model at inference time in web agents, using a judge model to evaluate simulated outcomes and trigger corrections. The distinction between CSG (post-execution anomaly detection via prediction-reality divergence) and WAC (pre-execution simulation + judge-based correction) is architecturally valid but conceptually narrow. Both use world models to decide 'when to intervene' during agent execution. The proposal should explicitly test WAC as a baseline to demonstrate the post-hoc approach is superior to the pre-hoc approach.", "Technical concern: Using sentence-transformer cosine similarity to measure divergence between predicted and actual A11y trees is an untested assumption. A11y trees are structured, semi-formal representations (role, name, value hierarchies), not natural language. Sentence transformers are trained on natural language sentence pairs. Tree-edit distance, DOM-diff metrics, or specialized structural similarity measures may be more appropriate. The ablation mentions BERTScore and token-level F1 as alternatives, but all are NLP metrics—none are designed for structured tree comparison.", "Missing citation: 'Agentic Uncertainty Reveals Agentic Overconfidence' (arXiv:2602.06948, Feb 2026) empirically shows agents are systematically overconfident (agents succeeding 22% predict 77% success). This directly motivates external verification gating and should be cited to strengthen the problem framing.", "The expected outcome ('CSG triggers verification at ~20-30% of steps, achieving task success within 1-2% of always-verify') is stated without justification. Where does the 20-30% estimate come from? If WebWorld's sycophancy causes most predictions to match reality (even when reality is wrong), the trigger rate could be much lower, with most errors going undetected. Conversely, if WebWorld's predictions are noisy on hard tasks, the trigger rate could be much higher (50%+), negating the efficiency gain.", "Cost realism: The proposal claims WebWorld-8B inference takes ~50-100ms per step. This seems plausible for short inputs, but A11y trees for complex web pages can be 2000-5000 tokens. At 8B parameters on A100, generating a comparably long predicted A11y tree (not just classifying) could take 1-3 seconds, not 50-100ms. The proposal should clarify whether WebWorld-8B generates a full predicted A11y tree or just an embedding/summary, and benchmark actual inference time.", "The Qwen3.6-27B model (released April 2026, Apache 2.0) supersedes Qwen3.5-27B and may be a stronger backbone choice. Not critical but worth noting for best experimental practice.", "Timeline: The 14-day ARR stretch goal is acknowledged as unrealistic, and AAAI 2027 is listed as primary target. This is honest but means the idea cannot be evaluated against the user's ARR May 25 deadline requirement."]
Feedback: The idea has a strong intuition (world model surprise as verification gate) and excellent competitor positioning, but needs targeted revisions:

1. **Address WebWorld sycophancy head-on**: This is the single biggest threat to the approach. Add a dedicated analysis: (a) measure WebWorld-8B's sycophancy rate on the calibration set by checking how often it predicts success when the agent actually fails, (b) report this as a key metric alongside ECE, (c) if sycophancy is high (>30% of error-steps get low-surprise predictions), propose a mitigation—either contrastive decoding against the sycophantic mode, or a simple 'surprise floor' that forces minimum verification rate on high-risk action types (form submissions, purchases, deletions). Frame the sycophancy finding itself as a contribution: 'we discover that world model sycophancy is a critical bottleneck for prediction-based verification.'

2. **Add WAC as a direct baseline**: WAC uses world models for web agent correction at inference time—it's the closest deployed system. Run WAC's approach on WebArena-VH and compare: does post-execution anomaly detection (CSG) outperform pre-execution simulation + judge correction (WAC)? This comparison would sharpen the contribution enormously.

3. **Validate A11y tree similarity metrics**: Before committing to sentence-transformer cosine similarity, run a pilot study comparing it against tree-edit distance on A11y trees and DOM-diff metrics. If sentence-transformer similarity fails to capture structural differences (e.g., a dropdown menu opening vs. closing), the gating signal will be unreliable. Consider linearizing the A11y tree into a canonical form before embedding.

4. **Justify the 20-30% trigger rate**: Either derive it from a pilot experiment on a small subset (e.g., 20 tasks), or present it as a variable to be measured rather than an expected outcome. The actual trigger rate is a key finding, not a prior assumption.

5. **Benchmark WebWorld-8B inference latency on real A11y trees**: Generate 50 sample A11y trees from WebArena tasks and measure actual generation time on A100/H100. If generation takes >1 second (plausible for long A11y trees), update the overhead analysis accordingly.

6. **Cite arXiv:2602.06948** (Agentic Overconfidence) to strengthen the problem motivation—agents are empirically shown to be overconfident, validating the need for external verification rather than self-assessment.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，
   不要只依赖搜索摘要。形成你自己对领域现状的独立判断。

3. **深度思考**：在修订之前，先独立思考以下问题：
   - 这个 idea 的核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach 来解决同一个核心问题？
   - 修订后的 idea 相比上一版有什么本质性的改进？

4. **避免表面修订**：如果你发现自己只是在换措辞或补充细节而没有实质改进，
   考虑是否需要 major revision 或 pivot。反复的 minor fix 不会拯救一个根基有问题的 idea。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，执行以下搜索流程：

1. **如果 reviewer 说'已有类似工作'**：
   - 搜索 reviewer 提到的论文，用 WebFetch 实际阅读
   - 搜索该论文的 cited-by，找到后续跟进工作
   - 明确你的 idea 与这些工作的差异化点——如果差异化不够，必须 pivot

2. **如果 reviewer 说'SOTA 过时'**：
   - 用 Papers With Code 查看当前排行榜
   - 搜索过去 6 个月的最新方法
   - 更新你的 landscape 和 baseline

3. **如果 reviewer 说'可行性有问题'**：
   - 搜索类似规模实验的实际成本和时间线
   - 搜索 GitHub 上是否有可复用的实现
   - 搜索相关数据集/模型的可获取性

4. **如果 reviewer 说'novelty 不足'**：
   - 对核心方法尽量做 3-5 种不同关键词组合的搜索
   - 搜索相邻领域是否有类似思路
   - 如果确实 novelty 不足，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- Use WebSearch to find updated information if the reviewer flagged outdated claims.
- You have full freedom in how much to change:
  - Minor fix: if only specific details are wrong, correct them and keep everything else.
  - Major revision: if the approach is fundamentally flawed but the core problem is valid, you may redesign the approach entirely.
  - Pivot: if the reviewer's feedback reveals that the core problem itself is invalid (e.g., the gap no longer exists), you may propose a RELATED but substantially different idea that builds on the same research area. This is preferred over forcing a doomed idea to pass review.
- The output replaces the original idea (same tracking ID). Whether you make a small tweak or a full pivot, output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields filled.
- In the output JSON, include a "change_type" field with one of: "minor", "major", or "pivot" to indicate the scope of your changes.
- Output the revised idea as a COMPLETE JSON object (same schema as original, plus "change_type").

## 停滞提醒
这个 idea 已经经过 3 轮修订，近 3 轮的平均分从 3.0 到 3.2，没有明显改善。

请认真思考：
- 当前方向是否存在根本性的瓶颈？反复的 minor fix 是否在回避核心问题？
- 如果你认为问题出在 approach 而非 framing，可以做 major revision。
- 如果你认为 core problem 本身就有问题（gap 不存在、问题不够重要），pivot 到同一研究领域下的新方向可能是更好的选择。
- 当然，如果你有信心这一轮修订能实现突破，继续改进也完全可以。

最终由你判断——做你认为最能提升 idea 质量的选择。

Here is the report.

---

**Does the WebWorld paper explicitly acknowledge sycophancy?**

Yes. The paper explicitly uses the term "sycophancy" in two places. In Section 7 (Conclusions and Limitations): *"WebWorld has limitations. It exhibits sycophancy by generating overly optimistic outcomes that cater to the agent's action."* The Impact Statement repeats the concern: *"We also observe a sycophancy bias in the model's predictions, where simulated outcomes can be overly optimistic or cater to agent expectations, potentially hindering robust policy learning."* The authors recommend that practitioners *"apply additional domain-specific safety checks before deploying agents trained on WebWorld in high-stakes environments"* and encourage the community to develop *"adversarial robustness mechanisms, and alignment methods to reduce sycophancy."*

**Are there known techniques for mitigating sycophancy in world model predictions?**

Several approaches exist, though none are purpose-built for world-model sycophancy specifically. Sycophancy-aware contrastive decoding (published early 2026) recalibrates token-level output distributions by contrasting responses to neutralized vs. leading queries -- a training-free, inference-time method shown effective on vision-language models. The CONSENSAGENT framework dynamically refines prompts in multi-agent settings to reduce sycophancy. More broadly, supervised fine-tuning with LoRA on debiased instruction datasets can mitigate extrapolation bias at the parameter level.

**Is there work on contrastive or adversarial approaches to fix world model optimism?**

Yes, from two angles. Villaflor et al. ("Addressing Optimism Bias in Sequence Modeling for Reinforcement Learning," ICML 2022) explicitly disentangle policy and world dynamics to prevent overly optimistic behavior in offline RL. Conversely, "Optimistic World Models" (arXiv:2602.10044) deliberately introduces an optimistic dynamics loss for exploration in sparse-reward settings -- showing optimism can be a feature or a bug depending on context. Regularized Contrastive Decoding (RCD) learns diverse hallucination patterns via adversarial-aware fine-tuning and contrasts them at inference time, and is directly applicable to overoptimistic generation.

**Summary:** WebWorld is one of the first world models to explicitly name sycophancy as a failure mode. The bias causes the simulator to predict success when the agent acts, rather than accurately modeling failures. Mitigation remains an open problem: contrastive decoding and policy-dynamics disentanglement are the most promising directions, but no published work yet applies these specifically to LLM-based world model sycophancy.

**Part 1: WAC (World-Model-Augmented Web Agents with Action Correction, arXiv:2602.15384)**
1. WebFetch https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15384 and extract:

   - What are WAC's results on WebArena or similar benchmarks?
   - What are WAC's limitations?

**Part 2: A11y tree / DOM similarity metrics**
2. WebSearch for "accessibility tree comparison metric similarity DOM" and "tree edit distance DOM web testing 2025 2026"
3. WebSearch for "A11y tree similarity web agent evaluation metric"
4. WebSearch for "structural similarity HTML DOM comparison automated testing"

Report:
- WAC's exact mechanism (how it uses world models at inference time)

content.text:
Here is the consolidated report.

---

## WAC Mechanism

WAC uses a **two-stage inference pipeline**, both pre-execution:

**Stage I (Guidance):** A router decides if world-model guidance is needed. If so, the world model (an LLM -- Qwen3-VL-Plus, not a separately trained model) provides high-level textual guidance that the action model incorporates when proposing candidate actions.

**Stage II (Simulation + Judging):** For each candidate action, the world model predicts the next observation as a natural-language description: `o^(t+1) = W(o_t, a_t)`. A judge model then scores each simulated outcome on a discrete scale {0, 0.5, 1} using predefined questions (not free-form generation). If all candidates score below threshold theta=0.4, corrective feedback loops back to Stage I for refinement. Crucially, WAC never compares predicted vs. actual post-execution states -- all simulation is pre-execution.

**Results:** 24.5% on VisualWebArena (+1.8% over WebDreamer), 16.0% on Online-Mind2Web (+1.3%). **Limitations:** simulation fidelity gaps, dependence on base model capabilities, and no fine-tuning.

## A11y Tree / DOM Comparison Metrics

**Sentence-transformer embeddings** are not well-supported in literature for A11y tree comparison. The literature strongly favors **structural metrics**:

- **Tree Edit Distance (TED):** The canonical approach (Zhang-Shasha 1989, RTED). Counts minimum node insertions, deletions, and relabelings. Directly applicable to A11y trees as ordered labeled trees. GTED (Generalized TED) was recently proposed for tree-structured evaluation.
- **SFTM (Similarity-based Flexible Tree Matching):** Uses node labels and local topology similarity; faster than exact TED for large trees.
- **html-similarity library** ([PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/html-similarity/)): Computes structural similarity via longest common subsequence of serialized tag sequences: `(2 * LCS) / (|A| + |B|)`. Combines with style similarity using a tunable weight.
- **jqgram** ([GitHub](https://github.com/hoonto/jqgram)): JavaScript PQ-gram approximation of tree edit distance, works on arbitrary tree implementations including DOM.

**No existing implementation** specifically targets A11y tree similarity as an evaluation metric for web agents. The closest tools operate on DOM/HTML trees. Adapting TED or PQ-gram distance to A11y trees (using role, name, state as node labels) would be straightforward and better grounded than embedding-based approaches, which discard structural/hierarchical information.

Sources:
- [WAC paper (arXiv:2602.15384)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15384)
- [SFTM paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.12821)
- [html-similarity (GitHub)](https://github.com/matiskay/html-similarity)
- [jqgram (GitHub)](https://github.com/hoonto/jqgram)
- [RTED algorithm](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.14778/2095686.2095692)
- [GTED (Generalized Tree Edit Distance)](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.07399v1)
- [Similo: similarity-based web element localization](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3571855)
- [Tree Edit Distance database (Salzburg)](https://tree-edit-distance.dbresearch.uni-salzburg.at/)

Here is the consolidated report:

---

**1. Agentic Overconfidence (arXiv:2602.06948)**

The paper finds that AI agents systematically overestimate success likelihood. The headline figure: some agents succeeding only 22% of the time predicted 77% success -- a 55-point calibration gap. Methodology involves eliciting success probabilities before, during, and after task execution. Key finding on external verification: pre-execution assessment with strictly less information tends to yield better discrimination than standard post-execution review, though differences are not always significant. Their top recommendation is adversarial prompting -- reframing assessment as "bug-finding" -- which achieves the best calibration.

**2. Qwen3.6-27B**

Confirmed released April 22, 2026 on HuggingFace and ModelScope under Apache 2.0. It is a dense 27B-parameter model with 262K context (extensible to 1M), native multimodal support (text/image/video), and a "Thinking Preservation" mechanism. vs. Qwen3.5: it surpasses the previous flagship Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (an 807GB MoE model) across all major coding benchmarks while being only 55.6GB. Two weight variants available: BF16 and FP8, compatible with SGLang, vLLM, KTransformers, and HF Transformers.

**3. WebArena SOTA**

As of May 2026: Claude Mythos Preview leads at 68.7%, GPT-5.4 Pro at 65.8%, Claude Opus 4.6 at 64.5%. Human baseline is ~78%. The top-10 spread is 16.6 points. WebArena Verified (on PyPI since Jan 2026) audits all 812 tasks with normalization-aware comparators, reducing false negatives by ~11%. The Verified-Hard subset is 258 tasks, cutting runtime by 68.2% while preserving discriminative power. Note: a 2026 Berkeley RDI study found several agent benchmarks including WebArena can be exploited to near-perfect scores without solving tasks.

**4. Prediction-Observation Mismatch (arXiv:2503.02552)**

The paper uses world models to continuously monitor discrepancies between predicted and observed system behavior during inference; when mismatches exceed an error threshold, safety measures (e.g., emergency stops) trigger. Demonstrated on recognizing changes in robot geometry, gravitational magnitude shifts, and unexpected forces on a quadcopter. Specific threshold values are in the full paper, not the abstract. The paper focuses on robotics/RL policies, not LLM agents. ## Sycophancy Mitigation with Contrastive Decoding

Research has systematically analyzed sycophancy across multiple vision-language benchmarks and proposes an inference-time mitigation framework that is training-free and model-agnostic.

A contrastive decoding mechanism dynamically recalibrates the token-level output distributions by contrasting responses to both neutralized and original leading queries. More specifically, the approach employs a query neutralizer leveraging a language model to suppress implicit sycophantic bias in user queries, then introduces a sycophancy-aware contrastive decoding mechanism that dynamically recalibrates token-level output distributions.

## Leading Query Contrastive Decoding (LQCD)

Leading Query Contrastive Decoding (LQCD) suppresses sycophantic tokens at decode time, effectively reducing undue conformity without harming performance.

## Related Contrastive Decoding Applications

The contrastive decoding approach has also been adapted for other model issues. Training-free solutions like contrastive decoding achieve hallucination mitigation by subtracting the estimated hallucination pattern from a distorted input, though these handcrafted perturbations may poorly capture authentic hallucination patterns.

For complex web pages (2000–5000 token A11y trees), generation takes ~1–3 seconds on A100—significant per-step overhead that we account for in the cost analysis.

For each step, we classify the world model's prediction as 'success-aligned' (predicted A11y tree consistent with action succeeding) or 'failure-aligned' (consistent with action failing or unexpected outcome), then compare against actual step outcomes. We compute: (a) **Sycophancy Rate (SR)**: fraction of error-steps where WebWorld predicts a success-aligned outcome, stratified by action type (navigation, form-fill, click, type, scroll); (b) **Sycophancy-Conditional Surprise Distribution**: the distribution of surprise scores on error-steps, revealing the blind spot magnitude. We hypothesize SR will be highest for form submissions and confirmation-requiring actions. PQ-gram profiles are computed for both predicted and actual A11y trees, yielding a normalized structural distance in O(n log n) time (<5ms for typical A11y trees). This captures structural changes (elements appearing/disappearing, tree reorganization) that embedding-based metrics miss.

However, because sycophancy is a directional content bias (not a confidence magnitude issue), calibration alone is insufficient. We add two sycophancy-specific mitigations:

(a) **Action-Type-Stratified Thresholds**: On the calibration set, we learn separate gating thresholds per action-type group. Action types with high measured SR (from the audit) receive lower surprise thresholds (more aggressive verification). This directly compensates for sycophancy-induced surprise suppression on high-risk actions.

(b) **Surprise Floor**: For action types where SR exceeds a critical level (e.g., >40%), we impose a minimum verification rate (e.g., verify ≥50% of such steps regardless of surprise score). This bounds the worst-case miss rate from sycophancy.

The gating decision combines three signals via logistic regression trained on the calibration set: (i) PQ-gram structural divergence, (ii) temperature-scaled prediction entropy, (iii) action-type sycophancy prior (SR from audit). Cost-sensitive threshold optimization minimizes λ_FP × FPR + λ_FN × FNR with λ_FN > λ_FP (missed errors costlier than unnecessary verification).

**5. Adversarial Verification Subroutine**: When gating triggers, we avoid free-form self-rechecking (which is confirmatory per arXiv:2602.03485) and open-ended 'did I make a mistake?' prompts. Instead, inspired by arXiv:2602.06948's finding that adversarial 'bug-finding' framing achieves best calibration, we present the backbone with: (a) a structured PQ-gram-derived diff highlighting specific structural discrepancies between predicted and actual A11y trees, and (b) an adversarial prompt: 'Find the bug: the world model expected [predicted subtree] but the page shows [actual subtree]. Is this a problem for the current task?' This focused, adversarial framing resists confirmation bias.

**6. Overhead Analysis (Honest Estimates)**: WebWorld-8B generates a full predicted A11y tree, which for complex pages (2000–5000 tokens) takes ~1–3 seconds on A100. PQ-gram computation adds <5ms. A backbone agent step (Qwen3.6-27B) with browser interaction takes 3–10 seconds. Thus SASG adds ~15–30% per-step latency overhead for the prediction alone. Full verification (an additional backbone call with adversarial prompt) costs 3–10 seconds and triggers at a subset of steps. If SASG triggers verification at ~X% of steps (X is a measured outcome, not a prior assumption), net compute compared to always-verify is: (1–3s prediction overhead) + (X% × 3–10s verification) vs. (100% × 3–10s verification). For SASG to provide net savings over always-verify, X must be below ~70–80%. We report the actual trigger rate as a key finding. Even if compute savings are modest, the primary value proposition is TARGETING verification at the right steps (improving verification precision), not merely reducing verification frequency.

**7. Evaluation**: WebArena Verified-Hard (258 tasks, publicly available via PyPI webarena-verified) using Qwen3.6-27B (released April 2026, Apache 2.0) as the primary backbone agent.
